source_text: Κἂν λέγῃ τις οὐρανοὺς μὲν εἶναι τὰς θεωρητικὰς δυνάμεις, στερέωμα δὲ τὰς πρακτικὰς καὶ ποιητικὰς τῶν καθηκόντων, ὡς κεκομψευμένον μὲν τὸν λόγον ἀποδεχόμεθα, ἀληθῆ δὲ εἶναι οὐ πάνυ τι δώσομεν. Οὕτω γὰρ ἂν καὶ δρόσος, καὶ πάχνη, καὶ ψῦχος, καὶ καῦμα, ἐπειδὴ ὑμνεῖν παρὰ τῷ Δανιὴλ τὸν τῶν ὅλων δημιουργὸν ἐπετάχθη, νοερά τις ἔσται καὶ ἀόρατος φύσις. Ἀλλ' ὁ ἐν τούτοις λόγος παρὰ τῶν νοῦν ἐχόντων τεθεωρημένως ἐκλαμβανόμενος, συμπληρωτικός ἐστι τῆς δοξολογίας τοῦ κτίσαντος. Οὐ μόνον γὰρ τὸ ἐπάνω τῶν οὐρανῶν ὕδωρ, ὡς προηγούμενον ταῖς τιμαῖς διὰ τὴν ἐξ ἀρετῆς προσοῦσαν αὐτῷ ὑπεροχὴν τῷ Θεῷ τὸν αἶνον ἀποπληροῖ, ἀλλ', Αἰνεῖτε γὰρ αὐτὸν, φησὶ, καὶ τὰ ἐκ τῆς γῆς, δράκοντες καὶ πᾶσαι ἄβυσσοι. Ὥστε καὶ ἡ ἄβυσσος, ἣν εἰς τὴν χείρονα μοῖραν οἱ ἀλληγοροῦντες ἀπέρριψαν, οὐδὲ αὐτὴ ἀπόβλητος ἐκρίθη τῷ ψαλμῳδῷ, εἰς τὴν κοινὴν τῆς κτίσεως χοροστασίαν παραληφθεῖσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὴ κατὰ τοὺς ἐνυπάρχοντας αὐτῇ λόγους ἁρμονίως συμπληροῖ τὴν ὑμνῳδίαν τῷ ποιητῇ. 3.10 Καὶ εἶδεν ὁ Θεὸς ὅτι καλόν. Οὐχὶ ὀφθαλμοῖς Θεοῦ τέρψιν παρέχει τὰ παρ' αὐτοῦ γινόμενα, οὐδὲ τοιαύτη παρ' αὐτῷ ἡ ἀποδοχὴ τῶν καλῶν, οἵα καὶ παρ' ἡμῖν· ἀλλὰ καλὸν τὸ τῷ λόγῳ τῆς τέχνης ἐκτελεσθὲν, καὶ πρὸς τὴν τοῦ τέλους εὐχρηστίαν συντεῖνον. Ὁ τοίνυν ἐναργῆ τὸν σκοπὸν τῶν γινομένων προθέμενος, τὰ κατὰ μέρος γινόμενα ὡς συμπληρωτικὰ τοῦ τέλους, τοῖς τεχνικοῖς ἑαυτοῦ λόγοις ἐπελθὼν ἀπεδέξατο. Ἐπεὶ καὶ χεὶρ καθ' ἑαυτὴν, καὶ ὀφθαλμὸς ἰδίᾳ, καὶ ἕκαστον τῶν τοῦ ἀνδριάντος μελῶν διῃρημένως κείμενα, οὐκ ἂν φανείη καλὰ τῷ τυχόντι· πρὸς δὲ τὴν οἰκείαν τάξιν ἀποτεθέντα, τὸ ἐκ τῆς ἀναλογίας, ἐμφανὲς μόλις ποτὲ, καὶ τῷ ἰδιώτῃ παρέχεται γνώριμον. Ὁ μέντοι τεχνίτης καὶ πρὸ τῆς συνθέσεως οἶδε τὸ ἑκάστου καλὸν, καὶ ἐπαινεῖ τὰ καθ' ἕκαστον, πρὸς τὸ τέλος αὐτῶν ἐπαναφέρων τὴν ἔννοιαν. Τοιοῦτος οὖν δή τις καὶ νῦν ἔντεχνος ἐπαινέτης τῶν κατὰ μέρος ἔργων ὁ Θεὸς ἀναγέγραπται· μέλλει δὲ τὸν προσήκοντα ἔπαινον καὶ παντὶ ὁμοῦ τῷ κόσμῳ ἀπαρτισθέντι πληροῦν. Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἐνταῦθα ἡμῖν οἱ περὶ τῆς δευτέρας ἡμέρας καταληξάτωσαν λόγοι, ὥστε τοῖς μὲν φιλοπόνοις ἀκροαταῖς καιρὸν παρασχεῖν τῆς ὧν ἤκουσαν ἐξετάσεως, ὥστε εἴ τι χρήσιμον ἐν αὐτοῖς, τοῦτο τῇ μνήμῃ συσχεῖν, καὶ διὰ τῆς φιλοπόνου μελέτης, οἷον διά τινος πέψεως, τὴν τῶν ὠφελίμων ἀνάδοσιν ἀναμεῖναι· τοῖς δὲ περὶ τὸν βίον ἀσχολουμένοις δοῦναι σχολὴν διὰ τοῦ μέσου χρόνου τὰς φροντίδας διαθεμένοις, καθαρᾷ μεριμνῶν τῇ ψυχῇ πρὸς τὴν ἑσπερινὴν τῶν λόγων ἑστίασιν ἀπαντῆσαι. Ὁ δὲ τὰ μεγάλα δημιουργήσας Θεὸς, καὶ τὰ μικρὰ ταῦτα λεχθῆναι οἰκονομήσας, δώῃ ὑμῖν σύνεσιν ἐν παντὶ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ἀληθείας, ἵν' ἐκ τῶν ὁρωμένων τὸν ἀόρατον ἐννοῆτε, καὶ ἐκ μεγέθους καὶ καλλονῆς τῶν κτισμάτων τὴν πρέπουσαν δόξαν περὶ τοῦ κτίσαντος ἡμᾶς ἀναλαμβάνητε. Τὰ γὰρ ἀόρατα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθορᾶται, ἥ τε ἀΐδιος αὐτοῦ δύναμις καὶ θειότης, ὥστε καὶ ἐν γῇ, καὶ ἐν ἀέρι, καὶ ἐν οὐρανῷ, καὶ ἐν ὕδατι, καὶ ἐν νυκτὶ, καὶ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ, καὶ ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὁρωμένοις ἐναργῆ λαμβάνειν ἡμᾶς τοῦ εὐεργέτου τὰ ὑπομνήματα.
thought_title: Literal sense defended; God approves each work as good
orientation: Basil is closing Homily 3 on the firmament, rejecting allegorical readings of the waters above and explaining why God saw that the work was good.
pass_a_gloss: And if someone says that the heavens are the contemplative powers, and the firmament is the practical and productive powers of duties, we accept the account as elegant, but we will not at all grant that it is true. For in this way also dew, and frost, and cold, and heat, since they were commanded by Daniel to hymn the creator of all things, will be some intelligent and invisible nature. But the account in these matters, taken thoughtfully by those who have understanding, is a completion of the doxology of the creator. For not only the water above the heavens, as preeminent in honors because of the superiority belonging to it from virtue, fulfills the praise to God, but, 'Praise him,' it says, 'also the things from the earth, dragons and all deeps.' So that also the deep, which the allegorizers cast away into the worse portion, not even this was judged rejectable by the psalmist, having been received into the common chorus of creation, but also it according to the principles existing in it harmoniously completes the hymnody to the maker. 3.10 And God saw that it was good. Not to the eyes of God do the things made by him provide enjoyment, nor is the approval of good things with him such as also with us; but good is what was completed by the word of art, and what contributes to the usefulness of the end. He therefore, having set before himself the clear goal of the things being made, approved the things made in part as completing the end, having gone over them with his artistic words. Since also a hand by itself, and an eye separately, and each of the limbs of a statue lying divided, would not appear beautiful to the ordinary person; but placed into their proper order, the beauty from the proportion, scarcely ever, becomes known even to the layman. The craftsman, however, even before the composition knows the beauty of each, and praises each one, referring their thought back to the end. Such then indeed also now God is recorded as an artistic praiser of the works in part; and he is about to fulfill the fitting praise also for the whole world together when it is completed. But let our words about the second day end here, so as to give to the diligent hearers a time for examination of what they heard, so that if there is anything useful in them, to hold this fast in memory, and through diligent practice, as through some digestion, to await the distribution of the useful things; and to give to those busy about life leisure through the intervening time, having arranged their cares, to come with a soul pure of worries to the evening feast of words. And may the God who created the great things, and who arranged these small things to be spoken, give you understanding in everything of his truth, so that from the things seen you may understand the invisible, and from the greatness and beauty of the creatures you may take up the fitting glory about the one who created us. For his invisible things, understood from the creation of the world by the things made, are clearly seen, both his eternal power and divinity, so that both in earth, and in air, and in heaven, and in water, and in night, and in day, and in all the things seen we receive clear memorials of the benefactor.

choices.why: Literal rendering of the philosophical terms Basil attributes to allegorizers; 'powers' preserves δυνάμεις as faculties or capacities.

choices.english: practical and productive powers of duties
choices.why: Keeps the threefold distinction (theoretical/practical/productive) and the Stoic term καθήκοντα as 'duties'.
rejected: active and creative powers of obligations
practical and making powers of what is fitting

choices.english: is a completion of the doxology
choices.why: συμπληρωτικός means 'contributing to the fullness'; 'completion' captures the sense that the literal reading fills out praise of the creator.
The verb means to throw away or reject; 'cast away' preserves the force of dismissal into a worse category.
ἐναργής means vivid or clear; 'clear goal' renders σκοπός as the aim or end in view.
In the statue analogy, ἀναλογία refers to the proportional relation of parts; 'proportion' is the standard rendering.

bible_refs.note: Basil refers to the command in the Song of the Three Young Men that dew, frost, cold, and heat bless the Lord; the wording 'hymn the creator of all things' echoes the canticle's repeated 'bless the Lord'.
Basil quotes 'Praise him, also the things from the earth, dragons and all deeps' (Αἰνεῖτε αὐτὸν... δράκοντες καὶ πᾶσαι ἄβυσσοι), matching LXX Psalm 148:7.

Basil quotes 'For his invisible things, understood from the creation of the world by the things made, are clearly seen, both his eternal power and divinity' (Τὰ γὰρ ἀόρατα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθορᾶται, ἥ τε ἀΐδιος αὐτοῦ δύναμις καὶ θειότης).

pass_b_english: If someone says that the heavens are the contemplative powers and the firmament is the practical and productive powers concerned with duties, we accept the argument as elegant, but we will not at all grant that it is true. For by that logic dew, frost, cold, and heat—since they were commanded in Daniel to hymn the creator of all things—would be some intelligent and invisible nature. But when thoughtful people interpret the language in these passages with discernment, it is a completion of the praise of the creator. For not only does the water above the heavens fulfill its praise to God, as holding first place in honor because of the superiority it possesses from virtue, but, as it says, 'Praise him, also the things from the earth, dragons and all deeps' (Psalm 148:7). So even the deep, which the allegorizers cast away into the worse portion, was not judged rejectable by the psalmist, but was received into the common chorus of creation; and it too, according to the principles inherent in it, harmoniously completes the hymn to its maker.

And God saw that it was good. The things made by God do not provide pleasure to God's eyes, nor is his acceptance of good things the same as ours. Rather, what is good is what has been completed by the principle of his art and what conduces to the useful service of its purpose. So the one who set before himself the clear goal of the things being made, and who examined each thing made in its parts as contributing to the completion of that end by his own artistic principles, approved them. After all, a hand by itself, an eye on its own, and each of the limbs of a statue lying separately would not appear beautiful to just anyone; but when they are set in their proper order, the beauty that comes from proportion becomes evident, even to the untrained eye, though only with difficulty. The craftsman, however, knows the beauty of each part even before the composition, and he praises each individual part, referring his thought back to their end. Such, then, is the kind of artistic praiser of the individual works that God is now recorded to be; and he is going to complete the fitting praise also for the whole world together when it is finished.

But let our words about the second day come to an end here, so as to give the diligent hearers time to examine what they have heard, so that if there is anything useful in it, they may hold it fast in memory, and through diligent meditation—as through a kind of digestion—await the distribution of what is beneficial. And for those occupied with the affairs of life, let this interval give them leisure to set their cares in order, so that with a soul cleansed of anxieties they may come to the evening feast of words. May the God who created the great things and who has arranged for these small things to be spoken give you understanding in all his truth, so that from the things that are seen you may perceive the invisible, and from the greatness and beauty of the creatures you may take up the fitting glory concerning the one who created us. For his invisible things, understood from the creation of the world by the things made, are clearly seen, both his eternal power and divinity (Romans 1:20), so that in earth, in air, in heaven, in water, in night, in day, and in all things visible, we may receive clear reminders of our benefactor.

problems.quote: the practical and productive powers of duties
problems.source_quote: τὰς πρακτικὰς καὶ ποιητικὰς τῶν καθηκόντων
problems.why: τῶν καθηκόντων is 'of duties/appropriate actions', but 'powers of duties' is incoherent; should be 'practical and productive powers concerned with duties' or 'active and creative powers of moral conduct'
problems.fix: the practical and productive powers concerned with duties

problems.quote: what contributes to the usefulness of its end
problems.source_quote: πρὸς τὴν τοῦ τέλους εὐχρηστίαν συντεῖνον
problems.why: εὐχρηστίαν means 'usefulness/serviceableness', but 'usefulness of its end' is tautological; it means contributing to the useful service of the purpose
problems.fix: what conduces to the useful service of its purpose

edits.old: the practical and productive powers of duties
edits.new: the practical and productive powers concerned with duties

edits.old: what contributes to the usefulness of its end
edits.new: what conduces to the useful service of its purpose

fixed: Corrected 'powers of duties' to 'powers concerned with duties' to reflect τῶν καθηκόντων as duties/appropriate actions.
Corrected 'usefulness of its end' to 'useful service of its purpose' to reflect εὐχρηστίαν as usefulness/serviceableness and avoid tautology.

problems.why: τὸν ἀόρατον is neuter plural 'invisible things' (referring to God's invisible attributes), not masculine 'the invisible one' (person).
problems.ruling: τὸν ἀόρατον is masculine singular referring to God; next clause confirms with plural τὰ ἀόρατα αὐτοῦ.

edits.old: you may perceive the invisible one

fixed: Changed 'the invisible one' to 'the invisible' because the source 'τὸν ἀόρατον' is neuter plural, referring to invisible things (God's invisible attributes), not a masculine singular person.

problems.quote: Such, then, is the artistic praiser of the individual works that God is recorded to be
problems.source_quote: Τοιοῦτος οὖν δή τις καὶ νῦν ἔντεχνος ἐπαινέτης τῶν κατὰ μέρος ἔργων ὁ Θεὸς ἀναγέγραπται
problems.why: Word order garbled; 'God is recorded as being such an artistic praiser of the individual works'.
problems.fix: Such, then, is the kind of artistic praiser of the individual works that God is now recorded to be
problems.ruling: English word order makes 'artistic praiser' a predicate of works, not God; ὁ Θεὸς ἀναγέγραπται is subject.

edits.old: Such, then, is the artistic praiser of the individual works that God is recorded to be
edits.new: Such, then, is the kind of artistic praiser of the individual works that God is now recorded to be

fixed: The English word order was garbled; the source says God is recorded as being such an artistic praiser of the individual works. Inserted 'kind of' and 'now' to match Τοιοῦτος οὖν δή τις καὶ νῦν.

last_rejected.quote: as it says, 'Praise him, also the things from the earth, dragons and all deeps' (Psalm 148:7)
last_rejected.source_quote: Αἰνεῖτε γὰρ αὐτὸν, φησὶ, καὶ τὰ ἐκ τῆς γῆς, δράκοντες καὶ πᾶσαι ἄβυσσοι
last_rejected.why: Source has 'γάρ' (for), giving the reason for the preceding claim; English drops it, weakening the logical connection.
last_rejected.fix: For, as it says, 'Praise him, also the things from the earth, dragons and all deeps' (Psalm 148:7).
last_rejected.ruling: English 'as it says' naturally conveys γάρ's explanatory force; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.source_quote: Αἰνεῖτε γὰρ αὐτὸν, φησὶ, καὶ τὰ ἐκ τῆς γῆς, δράκοντες καὶ πᾶσαι ἄβυσσοι
last_rejected.why: Basil quotes Daniel for the command to praise, not Psalm 148.
last_rejected.fix: Daniel (cf. Daniel 3:57 LXX, the Song of the Three Youths)
last_rejected.ruling: Daniel reference is for ὑμνεῖν...ἐπετάχθη earlier; Psalm 148:7 correctly cites δράκοντες καὶ πᾶσαι ἄβυσσοι.

last_rejected.quote: as holding first place in honor because of the superiority it possesses from virtue
last_rejected.source_quote: ὡς προηγούμενον ταῖς τιμαῖς διὰ τὴν ἐξ ἀρετῆς προσοῦσαν αὐτῷ ὑπεροχὴν
last_rejected.why: Misreads προηγούμενον as 'holding first place' rather than 'going before/leading'; ἀρετῆς here likely refers to the water's natural excellence, not moral virtue.
last_rejected.fix: as taking the lead in honors because of the superiority present in it from its excellence
last_rejected.ruling: 'Holding first place' is within προηγούμενον's range; 'virtue' for ἀρετῆς is standard. Mere preference, not error.
